title: Wide Field Imager view of the spiral galaxy NGC 247
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 247, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope
celestial: NGC 247 · constellation Cetus · about 11 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This is the spiral galaxy NGC 247, photographed with the Wide Field Imager at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. Its distance is thought to be about 11 million light-years, and it sits in Cetus, the Whale.

That makes NGC 247 one of the closest galaxies to our Milky Way. Nearness matters in astronomy, because the closer a galaxy is, the more detail telescopes can resolve, from clusters of stars to clouds of gas.

NGC 247 is a member of the Sculptor Group, a small gathering of galaxies held together by gravity. Galaxies rarely live completely alone, and most belong to groups or larger clusters, and those neighbors can influence how they grow and change. A spiral galaxy like this one is a flattened disc of stars, gas and dust with arms around a brighter center. The filters used for this picture include one that isolates the glow of hydrogen gas, which highlights regions where stars are forming.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (33.77 x 21.00 arcminutes) and distance (11 million light years), the frame spans roughly 108,000 × 67,000 light-years. Its light set out about 11 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This visible-light image was made with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope, using blue, visual and red filters plus H-alpha for glowing hydrogen. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, which could not see this galaxy in such detail.
